items.question: Which phonemes of the Mālinī are placed on the head, eyes, nose, seals, and ears?
premises: The letters na, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ are assigned to the crest and the head-garland.
The letter tha is assigned to the top of the head.
The eyes above and below receive other placements, ī is placed on the nose, ṇu and ṇū on the two seals, and the two ears receive their letters.
items.inference: Verse 121 continues the Mālinī nyāsa by mapping specific phonemes onto upper head, eye, nasal, seal, and ear locations.
uncertainties: The exact parsing of 'cordhve dho@nye' as applied to the eyes is compressed and may imply paired upper and lower eye placements.
The term 'mudre' may refer to specific ritual hand-seals or to bodily apertures; the nyāsa context suggests paired locations.
items.plain_english: Place na, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ on the crest and the garland of the head, and tha on the crown. Assign the eyes above and below, place ī on the nose, ṇu and ṇū on the two seals, and place the corresponding letters on the two ears.

items.question: How are the ba-ka group and related consonants distributed over the mouth, throat, shoulders, and arms?
premises: The ba-ka group together with i and ā is placed in order on the mouth, teeth, tongue, and palate.
The letters va, bha, and ya are assigned to the throat and the right and other shoulders.
The letters ḍa and ḍha are assigned to the two arms.
items.inference: Verse 122 extends the Mālinī nyāsa downward through the oral cavity, throat, shoulders, and arms in a fixed sequence.
uncertainties: The compound 'bakavarga+i+ā' is given in an analytical form in the tokenization; its exact intended segmentation follows the Mālinī sequence.
The long final compound compresses several placements; the mapping of va, bha, ya to throat and shoulders follows the transmitted reading.
items.plain_english: Place the ba-ka group with i and ā in order on the mouth, teeth, tongue, and palate. Place va, bha, and ya on the throat and the right and left shoulders, and place ḍa and ḍha on the two arms.

items.question: Which phonemes are assigned to the hands, branches, emblems, heart, breasts, and vital breath?
premises: The letter ṭha is placed on the two hands, jha and ña on the branches, and jra and ṭa on the trident and skull.
The letter pa is placed on the heart, and cha and la on the two breasts.
The letter mā associated with milk and sa joined with visarga are identified with the life-breath.
items.inference: Verse 123 maps further Mālinī phonemes onto the hands, emblems, chest, and the vital breath.
uncertainties: The terms 'śākhā' and 'śūlakapālake' may refer to bodily extensions and iconographic emblems; the nyāsa reading allows both ritual and embodied reference.
The phrase 'kṣīramā sa jīvo visargayuk' is compact; it likely identifies mā and saḥ with the vital current.
items.plain_english: Place ṭha on the two hands, jha and ña on the branches, and jra and ṭa on the trident and skull. Place pa on the heart and cha and la on the two breasts. Mā, associated with milk, and sa joined with visarga are said to be the life-breath.

items.question: How are ha, ṣa, kṣa, and the group ending with ma placed on the breath and lower body?
premises: The letter ha is declared to be the vital breath.
The letters ṣa and kṣa are placed on the belly and the navel.
The group ending with ma goes to the hips, private parts, and pair of thighs, and likewise to the two knees.
items.inference: Verse 124 completes the lower-body mapping of the Mālinī nyāsa from the vital breath down to the knees.
uncertainties: The exact members of 'maśāntā' depend on the Mālinī sequence and are not individually listed in this verse.
The distribution of that group across hips, private parts, thighs, and knees is stated collectively rather than one-to-one.
items.plain_english: Ha is declared to be the vital breath. Ṣa and kṣa go to the belly and the navel. The group ending with ma goes to the hips, the private parts, and the pair of thighs, and likewise to the two knees.

items.question: How does the Mālinī nyāsa conclude on the legs and feet, and what activates the goddess Mālinī?
premises: The vowels e and ai, and the pair following them, are placed on the two shins.
The letters da and pha are placed on the two feet.
This arrangement is the goddess Mālinī because she is stirred into activity by the possessor of power.
items.inference: Verse 125 closes the bodily placement sequence and identifies the completed phoneme arrangement as the activated goddess Mālinī.
uncertainties: The phrase 'tatparau' refers to the next pair in the Mālinī sequence; the verse assumes that sequence is known.
The identity of 'śaktimat' is not named here and may refer to Śiva or to the empowered practitioner.
items.plain_english: Place e and ai, and the pair that follows them, on the two shins, and place da and pha on the two feet. This is the goddess Mālinī, because she is stirred into activity by the possessor of power.

items.question: Why is the Mālinī body ultimately a body of Śakti rather than a mere phoneme arrangement?
premises: Through entry into ritual efficacy, that body becomes a body consisting of Śakti.
In ultimate truth, this Śakti-body arises from the mutual stirring of seeds and wombs.
That stirring is an emissive arising, not a merely mechanical combination.
items.inference: The Mālinī nyāsa produces a Śakti-body because the phonemic seeds and wombs mutually stir and give rise to emissive power.
uncertainties: The technical sense of 'bīja' and 'yoni' here spans phonemic, mantric, and cosmological registers.
The compound 'vaisargikodayāt' may emphasize visarga-based emission; the verse does not spell out the full mechanism.
items.plain_english: Because it enters into ritual efficacy, that body is, in ultimate truth, a body of Śakti. It arises from the mutual stirring of the seeds and wombs, through an emissive arising.
